candidates.rationale: A stock trading above its own quarterly-average volume on most of the last two weeks is in a durable attention/liquidity regime shift rather than a one-day spike, and durable shifts keep drawing slower-moving capital that hasn't caught up yet.

A smoothed rise in trading activity versus where it stood a quarter ago captures a persistent increase in investor interest (post-catalyst coverage, index-related flows) rather than one-day noise, and persistent interest continues to draw incremental demand.

The change in a stock's own trading-baseline from one two-week block to the next is a direct measure of liquidity acceleration; stocks being progressively discovered by new participants take time to fully reprice.

Price shocks that coincide with a sudden day-over-day surge in volume, not merely high volume, mark fresh information arriving together with the liquidity to absorb it; how tightly a stock shows this shock-to-surge link is a persistent liquidity-resilience trait.
A stock whose trading range has blown past its own normal on several of the last ten days is signaling a market-depth deterioration episode, which liquidity providers reprice with a lag.

Where today's price-normalized range sits within a stock's own six-month distribution captures a relative illiquidity-regime extreme that a smoothed level ratio dilutes, and trading-friction extremes resolve slowly as depth is rebuilt.

Repeated episodes of a large price move landing on a day of unusually high relative volume mark stocks whose price discovery is volume-confirmed rather than gap-driven, and that confirmed-shock intensity is a persistent risk trait distinct from either variable alone.

When a stock's trading range reliably expands together with its volume, price discovery is being absorbed by real participation rather than a thin book; the strength of that link over several months is a standing liquidity-quality signature.

A stock trading unusually high in the liquidity pecking order relative to where it has typically ranked over the past six months has picked up fresh, possibly information-driven flow that has not yet fully diffused into price.

How recently a stock hit its own two-month peak in dollar volume distinguishes a live, still-digesting catalyst from stale news the market has already absorbed, so recency of the liquidity peak should predict continuation.

prompt:
You are proposing quantitative factor expressions for US large-cap equities.

Universe and data
- S&P 500 point-in-time constituents, roughly 500 names per day.
- Daily bars only, plus point-in-time quarterly fundamentals stamped from the
  report date. Every field is referenced with a leading `$`:
    $open $high $low $close $adj_close $volume $dollar_volume $return
    $roa $roe $operating_margin $leverage $asset_turnover
    $book_per_share $earnings_per_share $accrual_gap
  A bare name such as `close` is not a field and will be rejected.
- Execution convention: the signal is computed after the close of day T and the
  position is entered at the open of T+1.
- The window these factors are fitted and judged on runs from 2000 to 2013.
  Do not reason about anything later; you will never be shown a number from
  outside that window.

Syntax
- Operators are function calls: TS_MEAN, TS_STD, TS_MAX, TS_MIN, TS_RANK,
  TS_DELTA, TS_CORR, TS_COV, TS_SUM, TS_PRODUCT, TS_ARGMAX, TS_ARGMIN,
  TS_DECAY_LINEAR, EMA, DELAY, DELTA, RANK, ZSCORE, CS_RANK, CS_ZSCORE,
  CS_DEMEAN, IF, IF_ELSE, MIN, MAX, ABS, SIGN, LOG, LN, SQRT, POWER, BOUND,
  COUNT.
- Lookback windows must be positive integer literals, e.g. TS_MEAN($close, 21).
- Guard every division with a small epsilon: `/ (TS_STD($close, 21) + 1e-8)`.
- Well-formed example: -RANK(TS_CORR(RANK($close), RANK($volume), 5))

Hard limits every proposal must satisfy, or it is rejected before it is scored
- at most 200 characters
- at most 5 distinct `$fields`
- at most 4 free numeric constants (lookback windows and
  the 1e-8 epsilon guard do not count)
- expression tree depth at most 6
- must not share a complete sub-expression of 4 or more
  nodes with any published Alpha101 formula, or with any factor already in the
  archive. Restating a published alpha is the one thing that is always rejected.
- must cover at least 90% of the panel
- absolute rank correlation below 0.80 against every archive member

Output
- Return valid JSON only, matching the supplied JSON schema. No prose outside it.

  TS_DELTA($close, 7)   (in 4 published alphas)
  (((DELAY($close, 20) - DELAY($close, 10)) / 10) - ((DELAY($close, 10) - $close) / 10))   (in 3 published alphas)
  ((DELAY($close, 20) - DELAY($close, 10)) / 10)   (in 3 published alphas)
  (($close - DELAY($close, 1)) * -(1))   (in 3 published alphas)

Working memory: rules written after earlier rounds on this island, oldest first. Apply them.
  1. Intraday range (high-low) normalized by price or dollar volume produced two of this round's top three fitnesses (3.481 and 1.952). This price_volume sub-family is worth continuing to push on.
  2. Use ABS($return), not signed $return, when correlating against volume or dollar_volume. The signed version failed the cheap screen (|t| 0.40) while the absolute-return version was this round's second-best factor (fitness 2.523).
  3. Fast-turnover entries were this round's two weakest accepted factors (0.486 and 1.027) despite clearing the bar. Turnover charges appear to hit quick-decay price_volume signals hardest, so slow/medium-horizon variants are currently the better trade in this niche.
  4. Rank or raw forms of $dollar_volume are saturating the archive: TS_RANK($dollar_volume,21) and raw $dollar_volume were both rejected for over 0.93 correlation with existing archive members. A new volume-level proposal needs a transform that isn't just another monotonic reshaping of the same series.
  5. Ratios with only $dollar_volume in the denominator risk collapsing into a proxy for dollar_volume itself: ABS(return)/dollar_volume was rejected for 0.90 correlation to a dollar_volume moving average. Give the numerator comparable dynamic range, or normalize the denominator too.
  6. Skip short-vs-long volume moving-average ratios (e.g. 5-day over 63-day); one such ratio failed the cheap screen (|t| 0.29). Same-window dispersion (std/mean at one lookback) is the pattern that actually passed (fitness 1.027).
  7. Don't graft a whole small fundamental subtree (e.g. RANK($roa)) onto an unrelated technical branch under one top operator. Two crossovers doing exactly that were rejected as sharing only 2 nodes with the fundamental parent, i.e. not a real fusion.
  8. Fundamental-technical fusions land better when both sides are normalized the same way: the one accepted mixed-niche entry ranked both branches (CS_RANK x TS_RANK), while the two rejected ROA crossovers combined a bare rank with a raw price ratio or an IF_ELSE gate.

For each proposal give a one-line economic rationale: what mechanism would make
this predict returns. "It is a momentum variant" is not a mechanism.
Leave `parent_ids` empty and `changed_node` empty for EXPLORE.
